newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia expected to weather Asian currency storm.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia expected to weather Asian currency storm.

text.p: Indonesia is expected to weather the Asian currency storm with the backing of sound economic fundamentals and conservative fiscal management by the central bank, economic analysts said on Monday.
The rupiah went for a roller-coaster ride against the dollar but stabilised around 2,456 to the U.S. currency in afternoon trading after bouncing between a low of 2,469 and a high of 2,445.
The stock market was generally flat, with a correction under way after hitting record levels over the past couple of weeks.
"We think basically the fundamentals look quite good," an analyst with a major Western bank said.
"The policy of the central bank, Bank Indonesia, is quite open and we shouldn't be too much affected," the analyst added.

Bank Indonesia widened its band against the dollar to 12 percent from eight last Friday in a move that took the market by surprise. This followed the de facto devaluations of the Thai baht and Philippine peso.
"The economic management is very sound," Sean Hughes, Indonesia country nmanager for Caspian Securities Jakarta, told Reuters.
"I think this widening of the band on the rupiah was actually quite a clever move and the timing was also very clever, so I think people are generally optimistic," he said.
The economy is officially expected to grow by over seven percent during the current calendar year, while inflation is currently below six percent year-on-year.
The government last week unveiled a new economic deregulation package, cutting tariffs on 1,600 items and moving to prevent a banking debacle by banning loans for land purchase and development.

An analyst with Vickers Ballas Tamara said the correction on the stock market had been predicted after the composite index hit record levels. It was hovering around 721.6 in late trading on Monday, marginally off the opening level.
"But we are still optimistic that the index will reach 775 points by the end of this year," the analyst added.
Brokers said the market was watching the rupiah closely, but the impact had not been significant.
Timothy Gray, president-director of PT Peregrine Sewu Securities, said there was a market belief that inflation was under control and the current account looked good.
"We're not seeing the same likelihood of a rush against the rupiah as we saw in the Philippines or in Thailand," he said.

"That being said, however, I think it (currency attacks) will have an impact. It will lead to some volatility in the currency and that undoubtedly is making foreign investors certainly cautious about all the markets in the region...," he said.
He said investors however were generally more comfortable with the Indonesian economy and currency.

"I think generally we're on the side of believing there's not going to be a significant move against the rupiah, but investors will be cautious for a period of time to see if enything does develop," he added.
